Bought the NordicTrack Commercial 1750 in January from the NordicTrack outlet store in Salt Lake City ($1,899 after their "New Year" discount). Nine months in, I'm on repair number two and I need to vent.

First issue hit in March: the incline motor started grinding on any setting above 5%, then just stopped responding. Took three weeks and four phone calls to get a tech out. He replaced the incline motor assembly under warranty, no charge, but I lost almost a month of my training block for a half marathon I was building toward.

Second issue started about two weeks ago — the belt started drifting to the left every time I ran past 6 mph, badly enough that my foot was clipping the side rail. Tech came out this past Tuesday (September 16th), re-centered and re-tensioned the belt, and told me the rear roller bearings were already showing wear "for a machine this age," which is not a sentence you want to hear nine months in.

The console, the iFit integration, the touchscreen — all genuinely great when the machine is working. That's the frustrating part. When it runs, it's a really good treadmill. But two hardware failures before the one-year warranty mark makes me nervous about what happens in month 13 when I'm paying out of pocket for parts and labor.

Anyone else have reliability issues with the Commercial series, or did I just get a lemon? Trying to decide if I push for a replacement unit or just ride out the warranty and hope for the best.
output:
Purchased the Nordictrack Commercial 1750 in January from the NordicTrack outlet in SLC ($1899 after the "New Year" sale). It's been 9 months now, and I'm on my 2nd repair. Need to vent.

1. March- Started having problems with incline motor grinding at incline above 5%. Stopped working all together. Had to schedule tech to come out after 3 weeks and 4 phone calls. Tech came out and replaced incline motor assembly under warranty (no cost). However, it cost me almost 1 month of training for half-marathon I was preparing for.

2. ~2 weeks ago- Belt was starting to pull to the left when I ran above 6mph. Enough to where my foot was catching the side rail. Tech came out last Tuesday (9/16). Tech re-centered and re-tensioned the belt. Told me rear roller bearings were showing wear "for a machine this age" (9 months). Yikes....

I love the console. I love integration with iFit. I love the touch screen. It is all awesome when it works. And that's the rub. It's a pretty damn good treadmill when it works. But to have 2 hardware failures before year 1 of warranty. It makes me wonder how month 13 is going to go when I am having to pay for parts and labor.

Anyone else have any reliability issues with Commercial series? Or just a lemon?? Deciding to ask for new unit or just cross my fingers till warranty is out.

When the European Recovery Program—better known as the Marshall Plan—was signed into law by President Truman on April 3, 1948, West Germany's economic future looked bleak. Its industrial cities lay in ruins, its currency was nearly worthless, and its economy remained constrained by Allied occupation policies that had capped steel production and dismantled industrial plants. Yet over the next four years, roughly $1.4 billion in Marshall Plan aid flowed into what would become the Federal Republic of Germany, helping to catalyze one of the most remarkable economic recoveries of the twentieth century.

The aid itself, distributed through the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), mattered less for its raw quantity than for its timing and function. West Germany received goods—cotton, wheat, coal, machinery—paid for in nearly worthless Reichsmarks, with the proceeds funneled into a special counterpart fund. This fund, worth several billion Deutschmarks, was later reinvested in infrastructure and industry, helping finance projects like electrical grid modernization and the expansion of the Ruhr Valley's steel sector. Perhaps just as important, Marshall Plan money covered Germany's chronic trade deficit in 1949 and 1950, buying the young West German state time while its currency reform of June 1948—which introduced the Deutschmark—took hold.

The Marshall Plan also forced institutional changes that proved decisive. Acceptance of American aid required participation in the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), pulling West Germany into a framework of European cooperation that would culminate decades later in the European Coal and Steel Community of 1951. Moreover, American pressure helped soften occupation restrictions: limits on steel production were progressively raised from around 5.8 million tons to over 11 million by the early 1950s, and plant dismantling largely ceased. Economist Ludwig Erhard, appointed Economic Director in 1948, combined this new freedom with his policy of the "social market economy," blending free-market competition with a social safety net.

The results were extraordinary. Industrial production in West Germany roughly doubled between 1948 and 1952, and by the mid-1950s the country was producing more than it had before the war—a phenomenon Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's government celebrated as the "economic miracle," or Wirtschaftswunder. Historians rightly caution that the Marshall Plan was only one cause among many, alongside currency reform, Korean War demand, and a skilled labor force. Still, it is fair to say that American aid did not simply rebuild West Germany's economy; it reoriented it—toward Europe, toward trade, and toward the stable democratic capitalism that would define the Federal Republic for generations.
output:
When President Truman signed the European Recovery Program (aka Marshall Plan) into law on April 3, 1948, the economic prospects for West Germany seemed grim. West German industrial towns were rubble. The currency was practically worthless. And the economy remained shackled to occupation-era Allied policy limiting steel output and breaking up industrial facilities. But in the succeeding four years, West Germany (soon to become the Federal Republic) received about $1.4 billion in Marshall Plan aid that catalyzed one of the most stunning economic comebacks of the 20th century.

The Marshall Plan aid provided by the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) had less to do with the size of the aid than with its timing and function. The Marshall Plan provided goods (cotton, wheat, coal, machinery, etc.) to West Germany which were purchased with virtually worthless Reichsmarks that were in turn deposited in a special counterpart fund. That fund, a few billion Deutschmarks, was in turn invested in infrastructure and industry to support such things as the modernization of the electrical grid and expansion of the steel industry in the Ruhr Valley. And perhaps equally important was the Marshall Plan aid which in 1949 and 1950 helped support Germany's persistent trade deficit, giving breathing room to the young West German government during the adjustment period of its currency reform in June 1948 (which introduced the Deutschmark).

The Marshall Plan also led to important institutional changes. In order to receive US aid, West Germany had to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), bringing West Germany into a European cooperation that led to the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community decades later. Also, US pressure relaxed some occupation restrictions, incrementally boosting the steel production quota from about 5.8 million tons to over 11 million tons by the early 1950s, while dismantling industrial plants was more or less stopped. Meanwhile, the new Economic Director (1948) Ludwig Erhard combined these new opportunities with his policy of the "social market economy," which integrated free-market competition with social safety-nets.

Between 1948 and 1952, West German industrial production approximately doubled. By the mid-1950s West Germany was producing more than it did before the war. The Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's government called this phenomenon the "economic miracle" (Wirtschaftswunder). Of course, historians are careful to note that the Marshall Plan was only one of several reasons for West Germany's recovery (the others being the currency reform, the Korean War-driven demand, and the availability of skilled labor). But it's fair to say that the US aid didn't only repair West Germany's economy, it re-directed the economy. Re-directed towards Europe, trade and stable, democratic capitalism that was to be the Federal Republic's hallmark for decades to come.

The best fix is to reduce how often two people edit the same lines, not to rely on Git’s conflict resolution.

For example, in our `checkout-web` repository, Maya owns the `CartSummary.jsx` layout and Jordan owns the tax-calculation hook. We split the component into smaller files:

```text
CartSummary/
CartSummary.jsx
useCartTotals.js
CartLineItem.jsx
CartSummary.test.jsx
```

Each person works on a short-lived branch such as `maya/cart-layout` or `jordan/tax-hook`, and branches from `main` immediately before starting. We open pull requests within one or two days instead of keeping branches for weeks. Before opening a PR, we run:

```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
npm test -- CartSummary
```

The component should also receive data through props rather than having multiple developers modify shared internal logic. For instance, `CartSummary.jsx` can render `subtotal`, `tax`, and `total`, while `useCartTotals.js` calculates those values. That lets Jordan change calculations without touching Maya’s JSX.

If two changes genuinely must affect the same lines, agree on the integration order. On September 21, 2026, for example, Maya’s structural refactor should merge first; Jordan can then rebase onto it and update the hook’s interface. Avoid resolving the conflict independently in both branches.

Finally, make commits small and focused. A commit named `Extract CartLineItem` is much easier to review and rebase than one containing formatting changes, dependency upgrades, and business logic. Enable branch protection and require a successful CI check so the second PR is tested against the current `main` before merging.
output:
Don't try to make Git handle conflicts, try to minimize the number of lines being changed by two different people.

For example, in our checkout-web repo, Maya is in charge of the layout of `CartSummary.jsx` and Jordan is in charge of the tax calculation hook. We split the component into several files.

```text
CartSummary/
CartSummary.jsx
useCartTotals.js
CartLineItem.jsx
CartSummary.test.jsx
```

Maya and Jordan each create short-lived branches (like `maya/cart-layout` or `jordan/tax-hook`). They branch off `main` just before they begin. We create pull requests within a day or two, rather than letting branches live for weeks. We run this before we create the PR:

```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
npm test -- CartSummary
```

Also, supply the component with data from props, rather than letting many developers change the same internal code. For example, let `CartSummary.jsx` display `subtotal`, `tax`, and `total`. Let `useCartTotals.js` handle the calculation. This way, Jordan can alter the calculations without disturbing Maya's JSX.

If you really have to change the same lines of code, at least coordinate the order in which you will integrate the changes. Suppose it's September 21, 2026. Maya will merge her structural refactor. Then Jordan can rebase off of that and adjust the interface of the hook. Don't resolve the conflict from each of your branches.

Keep commits small and narrow. It's so much easier to read/rebase a commit like `Extract CartLineItem` than one that has some formatting, some dependency updates, some business logic. Turn on branch protection and enforce passing CI before they can merge. That way, the second PR is run against the latest `main` before it gets merged.

每年立冬前后，我妈都要上演一场“囤菜大战”。今年是100斤白菜、50斤土豆、20斤大葱，11月3号那天，她蹬着三轮车跑了三趟菜市场，跟摊主老王砍价砍到5毛8一斤，回家时棉袄都汗湿了。

我劝她：“妈，超市天天开门，何必呢？”她头也不抬：“你懂什么，1960年你姥爷拉着一车红薯干走三十里地去换粮，一家人靠这个过冬。”

后来我才慢慢理解。我妈1962年生在山东济宁的农村，小时候一年到头吃不上几顿白面，过年的饺子是地瓜面皮包的。她十几岁时最奢侈的梦想，是“顿顿有玉米饼子吃”。1980年她嫁到县城，第一件事就是托人买了两口大缸腌酸菜。那两口缸如今还在阳台立着，缸沿都磕出豁口了，她舍不得扔。

囤的不只是菜，是安全感。白菜堆在楼道，她每晚睡前都要去看一眼，像点验自己的士兵。邻居张阿姨笑她，转身自己也搬回来80斤。

有人说这是穷怕了的惯性。可我觉得，那是一代人把饥饿刻进了骨头里，又用一屋子白菜，笨拙地告诉自己：这下，饿不着了。
output:
每年立冬，我妈就上演一出“囤菜大戏”。今年100斤白菜、50斤土豆、20斤大葱。11月3号，蹬着三轮车去菜市场跑了三趟，跟摊贩老王杀价杀到5毛8一斤，回来棉袄都汗了。

我劝她：“妈，超市每天都有，犯不上。”我妈头也不抬：“你懂啥？你姥爷1960年拉着一车红薯干，走三十里地换粮，一家人就靠这过冬了。”

我后来才明白，我妈1962年生，山东济宁农村。小时候一年到头吃不上几顿白面，过年饺子也是地瓜面皮包的。她10几岁最奢侈的梦想就是，“顿顿有玉米饼子吃”。1980年嫁到县城，第一件事是托关系买了两个大缸腌酸菜。两个缸现在还在阳台立着呢，缸沿都磕豁了，舍不得丢。

这是在囤菜。同时也是在囤安全感。一堆白菜放楼道里，每晚睡前必须看看，就好像在点兵点将自己手下的兵。邻居张阿姨笑她，转头也屯了80斤。

说穷怕了的，惯性使然。其实是他们这代人的骨头里烙上了饥饿。用堆成一屋子的白菜，拙劣地给自己说，好了，这次，不会饿了。
